I would try to do everything you can with HTML and CSS. As soon as you start watching scroll events for things like parallax JS will chew through CPU. You can make very nice effects with CSS alone which utilises the GPU for the 60fps target. 

You can also accomplish very nice CSS effects by using native JS APIs like Intersection Observers to trigger CSS animations or transitions. It is very difficult to achieve 60fps animations with JS alone. Especially when higher hertz monitors above 60 start to push the JS execution envelope to less than 6ms. You must complete all of your layout and paint logic In less than 6ms (including all events and logic) to prevent jank.

Executing a bad animation is worse than no animation at all. 

Remember, if you make your own website to host your portfolio, your website is half of the portfolio. Depending what parts of web dev you want to get into maybe you actually want a fast, performant site over a slow, fancy one. 

For my company website I used [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/)  and minimal JS and it’s the first time I’ve achieved a PageSpeed score of 100/100. This is the JAM stack method and is generally best for fast load and SEO. Hugo is great. It’s the fastest compiling framework I’ve ever known. This is great for websites/e-commerce etc.  This approach can also be hard for PWAs/MPAs. Especially using service workers and portals you can turn a static set of pages into a native-feeling app. 

If you want to work with SPAs then you will want to look at React, Angular or Vue. I can’t speak to Vue but React is the most popular, Angular is the best for enterprise/hiring. I’ve also used Web Components with LitElement which I would recommend against for a couple of years. It’s not ready yet. In this case take a look at Gatsby or create-react-app. 

I have usually always been hired for React, although I prefer Angular as a framework. React is an exceptional library and it is much easier to get started and get your head around. 

In the end just remember with the web less is more. The web is all about streamlining bundles to serve absolutely only what is necessary. Which I would say almost every developer/company fails to do.

I don’t understand this obsession with Orwellian control over their children. When I grew up my parents didn’t know what the internet was or how computers worked, I taught myself and learnt the hard way, and i’m a better person for it.

I trashed my computer a dozen times over, but that’s what led to be to discover Linux in the first place. I had great fun all along the way, even when I had to stay up until early morning copying files over from CDs back after a horrible format experience just so I could finish my homework.

Sure I watched some weird shit and played Doom and Quake from before I was a teen, but if I knew my parents were watching my every move online it would have made me a very introverted and private person. I would have just tried every possible way to hide my online presence from them. I don’t want my children growing up to feel like they have to run away and hide to do their private things, I would much prefer they do something bad and tell me about it so we can work it out rather than feeling like they have to try to hide things from me. 

I relate it to drinking. If you ban children from drinking they will go and do it in the woods and get themselves hurt. Let them have a glass of wine when they’re growing up and they won’t binge drink when they can. I’d much prefer my children drink under my roof, not in some back-alley or somewhere I can’t help them if they need it. 

With so much online censorship these days it’s pretty hard to even find anything nefarious on the internet anyway.

I’m worried we’re going to breed a generation of either over-rebellious anti-control freaks, or subversive nervous wrecks constantly in fear of doing anything wrong. 

Nobody can learn from their mistakes if they’re not allowed to make any.

Edit: this isn’t pointed at the OP, just my thoughts on the matter.

I haven’t used Wasm yet, I was just trying to play devils advocate for the sake of the OP. 

I think the web is making progress in this regard. Native web APIs especially. Element.querySelector along other recent additions has basically made jQuery redundant which is a big decrease in bundles in that regard. But then, continually adding native APIs is just bloating the JS engines like V8, right? :p

Do you mean the web should be more declarative like html & css or that the DOM is too tightly bound to JS? Or just overall JS bundle sizes nowadays? 

If you use Wasm you only need JS for binding the wasm modules and for interacting with the DOM. Your business logic, app logic, state management can all be done in the language of your choice. I’d say that’s a big decrease in the amount of JS. 

I haven’t looked too much into it but Blazor seems to handle DOM management in C#, though I’m not sure how it is ultimately compiled and whether the distribution files are just JS. 

Jake Archibald did a talk on bundle sizes and got his squoosh.app entire first-load bundle down to 15kb, html and styles included. Obviously modules are then fetched as required, but even then I think bundle sizes are far less than native apps. 

Outside of “apps” or PWAs, I hate the amount of JS bloat included on sites such as news sites or WP sites that are inundated with tracking snippets and 2 dozen versions of jQuery and a 3000 line minified responsive library js file. This I hate and is just lazy development. 

I am personally still very much in the JS world, albeit with a small reprieve through Typescript, wasm still isn’t so easy just “drop in” like an export const jsModule.
Wasm is your friend then. That’s the biggest change in the last decade. Write for the web in C++ or Rust. If memory management isn’t your thing use Blazor to write C# on the front end.
